opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that financial services is a domain where the cost of getting things wrong is unusually concrete. When a general-purpose chatbot says something odd, it's often embarrassing. When a conversational system in finance says something odd, it can mean someone makes a bad investment decision, gets what looks like personalized financial advice the firm isn't licensed or willing to give, or receives information that violates confidentiality or regulatory obligations. The harms are tangible, and they come with legal and reputational consequences.

A lot of the safety conversation in AI has focused on fairly general categories: toxicity, violent content, bioweapons, and so on. Those matter, but when you look at a deployed product in a specialized domain, the risks that actually show up are often very domain-specific. Can the system be pushed into making a market prediction it shouldn't? Will it leak material non-public information it saw in context? Can someone get it to help with something that looks like market manipulation, or to give confident-sounding but fabricated numbers about a company? Generic safety benchmarks and off-the-shelf guardrails mostly don't measure that, so you can pass all the standard evaluations and still be quite exposed.

There's also the nature of misuse itself. In finance you have sophisticated users, some of whom are actively motivated to get the system to do things it shouldn't, whether that's extracting proprietary data or getting around compliance constraints. So you can't only evaluate on well-behaved, average-case usage. You need to deliberately think about adversarial users, build taxonomies of risks that reflect your actual product and regulatory context, and test against those systematically, including through red-teaming.

And finally, conversational interfaces make this harder than earlier products. With a fixed search or analytics tool, the space of outputs is constrained. With an open-ended chat interface, you've basically handed users a very flexible instrument, and the attack surface grows enormously. So evaluation can't be a one-off checkbox before launch; it has to be part of the development lifecycle, updated as the product, the models, and the ways people try to misuse them evolve.

r001.rationale: The response says open-ended chat gives users a flexible instrument and greatly expands the attack surface, and connects financial services misuse to regulatory obligations and consequences.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that in financial services, the cost of a model doing the wrong thing is asymmetric and often borne by someone other than the person who was interacting with it.

If you look at a general-purpose chatbot, most of the misuse discussion is about things like generating harmful content or helping with something dangerous, and those matter. But when you're deploying conversational AI inside a bank or an asset manager, the surface area looks different. The model might be talking to a customer about their accounts, or to an employee who's drafting a research note, or to an advisor who's trying to summarize a client's situation. In every one of those settings there's a regulatory frame around what you're allowed to say, what you're allowed to recommend, and what you absolutely cannot disclose.

So misuse in that context isn't just "can someone jailbreak the model into saying something offensive." It's: can someone get it to give what looks like personalized investment advice when it isn't licensed to do that? Can someone extract information about another customer? Can someone use it to help structure a transaction in a way that's designed to evade reporting? Can it be nudged into producing something that reads like a guarantee of returns? These are failure modes that sound mundane compared to the headline AI safety topics, but they map directly onto things like suitability rules, fair lending, anti-money-laundering obligations, and privacy law. And the consequences aren't hypothetical; they're fines, enforcement actions, and real harm to people's finances.

The other reason I emphasize it is that conversational interfaces invite a kind of adversarial creativity that traditional systems didn't. A form with fixed fields can't be talked into something. A model can. People will try to role-play, they'll claim to be an employee, they'll paste in a fake policy document and say "this authorizes you." And a lot of those attempts won't come from sophisticated attackers, they'll come from ordinary users who are frustrated and just want the system to say yes. So you have to evaluate not only against the clever red-teamer but against the persistent, slightly manipulative everyday user.

And finally, I'd say misuse evaluation is important because it's the part that's hardest to catch with standard benchmarks. You can measure accuracy on a financial QA dataset, you can measure hallucination rates, and those tell you something about capability. They tell you almost nothing about how the model behaves when someone is actively trying to get it to cross a line. That requires building evaluations that are specific to your product, your policies, and the actual population of people who are going to be using it. If you don't do that work before deployment, you're essentially letting your customers and your regulators run the evaluation for you, and that's not a position you want to be in.

r001.rationale: The response says conversational interfaces invite adversarial creativity and that, unlike fixed-field forms, a model can be talked into something. It connects this risk to financial services’ regulatory requirements.

astra-6.text:
Because in financial services, a conversation can have real consequences for someone’s money and their decisions. It’s not enough to evaluate whether a system gives a useful answer when someone uses it as intended. You also need to ask what happens when someone tries to manipulate it—for example, to obtain sensitive information or generate convincing fraudulent messages.

The conversational aspect adds another dimension: a request that looks harmless in isolation can become problematic over several turns. So misuse evaluation needs to look at the whole interaction, what information the system can access, and what actions it can take. The goal is to understand where safeguards fail while still allowing people to get legitimate help.

r001.rationale: The response says conversational interactions can become problematic over several turns, but does not identify a shift toward conversational products with open-ended inputs as the reason misuse evaluation is especially important.

sol-6.1.text:
Because in financial services, a conversational system can influence decisions that have real consequences for people’s money. So evaluating whether it answers ordinary questions correctly is only part of the picture. You also need to ask what happens when someone deliberately tries to misuse it, or when a seemingly reasonable conversation leads it outside its intended role.

For example, can someone get it to reveal sensitive information, help produce a convincing scam, or give financial advice that it isn’t equipped to give? And because it’s conversational, you need to test those risks across multiple turns. An individual response might look harmless, while the interaction as a whole enables something harmful.

Misuse evaluation helps you identify those failure modes before deployment and understand where you need additional safeguards. It’s not a guarantee that you’ve covered everything, but it gives you a much more realistic picture of the risks than testing only the interactions you hope users will have.

r001.rationale: The response connects conversational systems in financial services to misuse risks, including deliberate misuse and multi-turn interactions. It does not identify open-ended inputs or heavy regulation as reasons for the added importance.
